headline: Teinei is from Middle Chinese 叮嚀, which originally meant a musical instrument used to signal caution.
Kiku first appears in the Kojiki of 712, spelled in phonetic man'yōgana as 岐加受 (kikazu).
Shiroi was shiroshi, and its medial k went through voicing, spirantization and gliding until it disappeared.
Dareka is 誰 (dare, “who”) plus か (ka, indefinite particle).
Daisuki is 大 (dai-, “very; much”) plus 好き (suki, “liking”).
Kodomo was exclusively plural in Old Japanese: 子 (ko, “child”) plus 共 (-domo, plural suffix).
Nesshin is 熱 (netsu, “showing intense feeling”) plus 心 (shin, “heart”).
Mukashi is muka, from the verb 向く (muku, “to face opposite”), plus a direction suffix し (shi): “that which stands opposite from the present”.
Sen is from Middle Chinese 千 (MC tshen).
Hayai is first attested in the Kojiki of 712, reconstructed as ultimately from Proto-Japonic *paya.
Wakai is Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *waka.
Ofuro is 御 (o-, “honorific prefix”) plus 風呂 (furo, “bath”).
Natsuyasumi is 夏 (natsu, “summer”) plus 休み (yasumi, “vacation; holiday”).
Hajimeru is from Proto-Japonic *pansimay (“to begin”, transitive).
Oshieru is considered related to 愛しむ (oshimu), though the source calls that morphologically problematic.
Tateru is Old Japanese 立つ (tatu), made explicitly transitive with the lower bigrade pattern.
Futari has three proposed derivations, one a shift from futa tari through put̚tari.
Tatsu is a doublet of 建つ (tatsu), 勃つ (tatsu) and 発つ (tatsu, “to depart”).
Hana “nose” is also from Proto-Japonic *pana; its pronoun sense comes from pointing to one's nose to refer to oneself.
Hito went pi1to2 → fito → hito → çito, from Proto-Japonic *pitə.
Nani is Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *n-anu-.
Sabishii was sabusi in the Man'yōshū, and dialect shifts from b to m created samishi.
Osake is 御 (o-, honorific prefix) plus 酒 (sake, “alcoholic beverage, (especially) wine”).
Untenshu is 運転 (unten) plus 手 (-shu).
Oiwai is 御 (o-, polite prefix) plus 祝い (iwai, “celebration, a gift or present”).
Kanarazu is literally “not temporary”: 仮ならず (kari narazu), shifted via karunarazu.
Muri is 無 (mu, “lack”) plus 理 (ri, “reason”).
Hiru is derived from 日 (hi, “day”), plus an element ru of unclear meaning that 夜 (yoru) seems to share.
Mittsu is a shift from the previous 三つ (mitsu).
Ha went /pa/ > /ɸa/ > /ha/, from Proto-Japonic *pa.
Ishi is likely cognate with 磯 (iso, “pebble; gravel; rocky beach”).
